# 2 Kings 20: Research notes, verse by verse

**Gaps:** My tool limit ran out before I could check verses 14–18 and 20 in detail. I found nothing on the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Pentecostal sites (pneumareview, ag.org, samstorms), bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material, so those are left out. The only Catholic voice below is Haydock's commentary as hosted on studylight.org. The tradition labels (Baptist, Methodist and so on) are the ones studylight.org puts on each commentator.

---

**v. 1**
- **Meaning of "mortally ill":** The phrase points to a sickness no human could cure, literally "sick unto death." The phrase indicates a sickness that was humanly incurable—literally "sick unto death." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Warning, not fixed prophecy (Pulpit):** The statement was a warning, not a prophecy. It is parallel to that of Jonah to the Ninevites, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/20-1.htm)
- **Hidden conditions (Poole):** Threats like this, though stated absolutely, "have ofttimes secret conditions, which God reserves in his own breast." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
- **"Set your house in order":**
  - Wesley (Methodist) reads it as "Make thy will, and settle the affairs of thy family and kingdom." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
  - Keil & Delitzsch say it means giving orders about the household, not declare thy (last) will to thy family. (same URL)
  - Another note on the biblehub page says it was urgent because Hezekiah had not, as yet, any son; Manasseh, his heir and successor, not being born till three years after this time. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/20-1.htm)
- **Age:** Comparing 2 Kings 18:2 with 20:6, Guzik works out that Hezekiah was 39 years old when he learned he would soon die. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
- **Dating (scholars disagree):**
  - Ellicott (Anglican) ties it to the Assyrian invasion and suggests the illness may have been caused, or at least aggravated, by the intense anxiety which this grave peril created.
  - Constable dates it to the year Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem (701 B.C.) since Hezekiah died 15 years later in 686 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
  - Barnes puts it at 713 or 714 B.C. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/20-1.htm)
  - Coffman notes that capable scholars have dated it at several points between 713 and 701 B.C. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-5.html)
- **Source of the story (Pulpit, more scholarly):** Calling Isaiah "the prophet, the son of Amoz," as if readers had never met him, indicates the original independency of the narrative, which the writer of Kings probably obtained from a separate source. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/20-1.htm)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** He lists guesses about the illness, such as a pleurisy, a quinsy or the pestilence. He adds We should always bear in mind this awful warning. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)

**v. 2**
- **Turning to the wall:** The Pulpit Commentary says he turned away from the people at his bedside so he could pray without distraction. It was natural to Hezekiah, in every kind of affliction and distress, to take his trouble direct to God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-20.html)
- Keil & Delitzsch: it was the wall of the room, not of the temple (Chald.), i.e., away from those who were standing round, to be able to pray more collectedly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
- Guzik sees it as earnest, private prayer to God rather than to any man. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)

**v. 3**
- **Does Hezekiah plead his own merit? Commentators differ:**
  - Matthew Henry (on biblehub) says he is not claiming a reward as owed: it is Christ's righteousness only that is the purchase of mercy and grace. Henry also notes that Hezekiah does not pray, Lord, spare me; but, Lord, remember me; whether I live or die, let me be thine. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/20-1.htm)
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) admits the prayer can sound self-justifying. He says it was a valid appeal under the Old Covenant, with its blessings for obedience (Lev 26; Deut 28), but is not a fitting model for Christians, who pray in Jesus' name. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
  - Constable: God had promised long life to the godly under the Mosaic Covenant, and that promise was the basis of Hezekiah's appeal and God's answer. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
- **Why he wept:**
  - Keil & Delitzsch say early death in the prime of life appeared to the godly men of the Old Testament a sign of divine displeasure. He wept not only because he had no heir, but also because he was to die in the very midst of his life, since God had promised long life to the righteous. (same URL)
  - Pulpit: Human nature shrinks from death instinctively. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-20.html)
- **A dissenting note (Coffman):** Hezekiah would have been much better to have meekly accepted the Divine verdict on his illness, because three years later, during the extension of his life, Manasseh was born to him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)

**vv. 4–5**
- **Did God change his mind? (Matthew Henry):** God neither says and unsays. Rather, upon Hezekiah's prayer, which he foresaw and which his Spirit inclined him to, God did that for him which otherwise he would not have done. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_020.cfm)
- **"I will heal you" (Gill, Baptist):** God would heal him instantly, miraculously. Going up to the temple on the third day would show the cure to be miraculous. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/20.htm)
- **The third day (Pulpit):** It means thou shalt be so completely recovered as to be able to quit thy palace and pay thy vows in the courts of the Lord's house. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-20.html)
- **Was the first word false? (Guzik):** No. Hezekiah did in fact die – just not as soon as God first announced. Second, when God announces judgment it is almost always an invitation to repent and to receive mercy. Also, if Hezekiah had not made his passionate prayer, his life would not have been extended. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
- **What moved God (Precept Austin):** Tears did not draw God's response, but the sincerity of Hezekiah's heart did touch God's compassionate heart! (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Typology and prophecy readings:**
  - Kelly reads the episode as a type: in type, the true Son of David, the One on whom depend the deliverance of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Assyrian. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-3.html)
  - Gaebelein links the "third day" to Israel's future: For Israel there is also in store the third day, when they will be raised up nationally (Hosea 6:2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-kings-20.html)

**v. 6**
- **The fifteen years (Wiseman, quoted by Guzik):** since he died c. 686 b.c. this promise can be dated from about the time of the siege of Jerusalem. His recovery was also symbolic of the recovery of Jerusalem. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
- **Two linked promises:** one would confirm the other. When Hezekiah recovered his health, he could know that God would also deliver him from the Assyrians. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- Gill takes this verse to show the illness came before the destruction of the Assyrian army. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gill/2-kings-20.html)
- **"For the sake of David":**
  - Don Stewart says the prayer was answered because God had committed Himself to David. Since Hezekiah had no heir, the extra years kept David's line, from which the Messiah would come. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/26-did-hezekiah-convince-god.cfm)
  - Precept Austin adds a caveat: Not everyone agrees with the following statement but many reputable sources do agree. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Debate: does prayer change God's plan?**
  - **Reformed Baptist (Desiring God):** Asked whether Hezekiah changed God's mind: Ultimately, no, he did not. Yet God fought for the nation because Hezekiah prayed. And in doing so, God did exactly what he had always planned to do through prayer. (This is said of Hezekiah's prayer about Assyria, which v. 6 ties to this episode.) (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-difference-will-prayer-make)
  - **Open theism, as Stewart describes it:** On that view, the prayer of Hezekiah made the Lord change His mind and thus change His plans. Stewart argues against it: if God does not know the future, how could He guarantee that Hezekiah would live exactly that long? (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/26-did-hezekiah-convince-god.cfm)
  - **BibleHub Q&A (middle view):** Although from a human viewpoint this episode may seem like God changed His mind, the entire narrative fits within His eternal knowledge and sovereign purposes. (https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_2_kings_20_6_fit_with_omniscience.htm)

**v. 7**
- **Medicine and faith:**
  - Guzik: God can, and often does, bring healing through medical treatments, and apart from an unusual direction from God, medical treatment should never be rejected in the name of faith. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
  - Biblical Illustrator: Isaiah followed the best medical knowledge of his time. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html) It warns against those who make haste to conclude that, if the lump of figs healed Hezekiah, then God did not. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)
  - Matthew Henry: the figs might contribute something to the cure, but given how suddenly the disease was checked, the cure was no less than miraculous. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-3.html)
  - Coffman (earlier in his notes): God had called the illness fatal, yet Hezekiah did NOT hesitate to pray God for his own recovery. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
- **What the boil was:**
  - Matthew Henry suggests plague: The same disease which was killing to the Assyrians was trying to him. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
  - The Expositor's Bible calls it a carbuncle or imposthume. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-kings-20.html)
  - A physician writing at Precept Austin compares it to necrotizing fasciitis. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)

**v. 8**
- **Why ask for a sign:**
  - Gill: Hezekiah did not doubt the promise; he asked for the confirmation of his faith, as Gideon did. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/20.htm)
  - Knapp (quoted by Guzik): "Hezekiah quite properly asks for a sign to assure himself of his recovery. His hypocritical father, in mock modesty, refused to ask for a sign." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
  - Precept Austin: God does not rebuke Hezekiah for asking for a sign but graciously condescends to strengthen faith. It also warns that asking for signs is not a pattern for us today. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Order of events (Gill):** He renders it "had said": Hezekiah asked before the fig plaster was applied. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gill/2-kings-20.html)

**vv. 9–10**
- **Wording (Ellicott):** He suggests the Hebrew may be read as the shadow hath marched (or travelled) ten steps; shall it return ten steps? Going forward was "light" Because that was the ordinary course of things. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-20.html)
- **Why this sign fits (Guzik):** A shadow moving backward gave more time in the day, just as God gave Hezekiah more time. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)

**v. 11**
- **A miracle (Ellicott):** the sign is evidently regarded by the historian as something directly involving the Divine agency, i.e., as a miracle. (https://biblehub.com/2_kings/20-11.htm)
- **What the "stairway" was:** Ellicott favours Knobel's guess: a column rising from a circular flight of steps, probably visible to Hezekiah lying on his sick bed. (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-20.html)
- **How it happened (views differ):**
  - Ellicott lists theories: a mock sun, a cloud of vapour, an earthquake. (same URL)
  - The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: probably by refraction—none the less a Divine act. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-kings-20.html)
  - Patterson and Austel (quoted by Guzik) see no need for the earth's rotation to reverse, because the sign was noticed only "in the land." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)
  - Utley: Exactly how YHWH performed this miracle is unknown and really is not significant. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Where the dial came from (Gaebelein):** Ahaz may have brought scientific devices back from Damascus. It is impossible to determine whether this mode of measuring the progress of time (not strictly hours) was by a sun-dial. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-kings-20.html)
- **Hezekiah's poor response (2 Chr 32:25):** Hezekiah gave no return for the benefit he received, because his heart was proud. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)

**v. 12**
- **Why the envoys came:**
  - Clarke (Methodist) says Babylon had heard of the miracle; as we learn from 2 Chronicles 32:31. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-12.html)
  - Trapp (quoted by Guzik): "The sun - which was their god - had honoured Hezekiah; therefore they were sent to honour him too". (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_2Ki/2Ki_20.cfm)
  - Pulpit: the real tie was a shared fear of Assyria, but it was prudent to disguise this motive. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-20.html)
  - Precept Austin judges the underlying motive was intelligence-gathering. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
  - Bridgeway: Babylon was looking for allies to help it overthrow Assyria. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
- **Date (Pulpit):** The date of the embassy appears to have been B.C. 712, the year following on Hezekiah's illness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)

**v. 13**
- Gill: he showed his treasures in the pride and vanity of his heart. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gill/2-kings-20.html)
- Bridgeway: Hezekiah was proud of the prosperity he had brought to his kingdom, and was willing to cooperate, and Isaiah condemned foreign alliances. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
- Guzik calls it proud foolishness and the temptation of success. Knapp (quoted by Guzik) says it was worldly pride rather than spiritual pride. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-20/)

**vv. 14–18**
- **The fitting punishment (Matthew Henry):** It is just with God to take that from us which we make the matter of our pride. And the king of Babylon, with whom he was so fond of an alliance, should be the enemy. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_020.cfm)
- **v. 18, "eunuchs" (Clarke, via Guzik):** "Perhaps this means no more than that they should become household servants to the kings of Babylon. See the fulfillment, 2 Kings 24:13-15, and Daniel 1:1-3." (https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_2Ki/2Ki_20.cfm)

**v. 19: the clearest split among interpreters, even within one tradition**
- **Humble submission:**
  - Wesley (Methodist): I heartily submit to this sentence, as being both just, and merciful. Benson (also Methodist) says the same.
  - Ellicott (Anglican): Pious acquiescence in the will of God. He links it to the prayer "Give peace in our time, O Lord."
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (Presbyterian): a humble and pious resignation to the divine will.
  - (All at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)
- **Self-interested:** Clarke (Methodist) finds the question seems to be rather of an interested nature. He does not appear to deplore the calamities that were coming on the land. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kja/2-kings/20-19.html)
- **Mixed or mild:**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) says it was either resignation or relief. Relief would imply no very great defect of character in one who lived under the old Dispensation.
  - Pulpit: There may be a tinge of selfishness in his acquiescence, but it is not very pronounced.
  - Constable lists the options: he accepted God's will, or made a smug, self-serving comment, or that he took the message as a prayer that the disaster would be delayed.
  - (All at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)
- **Lange:** When God rebukes our vanity we should bow and call his word good, and after true repentance we may pray *Da pacem, Domine* ("give peace, Lord"). (https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/2-kings-20.html)
- **Catholic (Haydock):** He rejects the Jewish suggestion that Hezekiah did not care about his family, saying He is not indifferent about his family, as the Jews would insinuate. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)

**v. 20**
- The Biblical Illustrator draws a lesson: Hezekiah's "might" was diverted to the construction of "the pool and the conduit of water" for the relief of his people. In other words, he used peacetime for public good. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-19.html)

**v. 21**
- Gill notes that this verse does not say where he was buried; another book does. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-21.html)
- Josephus, quoted by Precept Austin, says Hezekiah lived fifty four years of his life, and reigned twenty nine. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
- **Manasseh:**
  - Guzik notes Manasseh was 12 when he became king, so he was born in the last fifteen years of Hezekiah's life. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-20-commentary)
  - Coffman calls Manasseh the very worst of all the kings of Judah! (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/20-1.html)
